Chapter 3: Questioning Faith, Family, and the Meaning of Obedience
As adolescence set in, everything started to feel a little different. The girl who used to find comfort in routine now felt the weight of expectations pressing down on her. What once felt safe and familiar—the rituals of family life—suddenly seemed like a set of invisible walls. And the faith her mother had passed down, filled with prayers and promises, just didn’t offer the certainty it used to.
In their home, religion was always at the center. Her mother, deeply devout and genuine, believed that faith was the foundation of a good life. She taught her daughter how to pray, how to show up at church, and—most importantly—how to accept the mysteries of belief without ever questioning them. For a while, the girl tried to go along, hoping that obedience would bring her the peace her mother kept talking about.
But as her mind grew more curious and restless, doubts began to sneak in. The stories of saints and miracles—stories she once accepted without thinking—now felt distant, maybe even a little unbelievable. The rituals felt empty, and the words of the prayers just echoed without meaning. She started to wonder: why does faith require so much submission? Why does it ask us to silence our questions and hide our true selves?
It wasn’t just religion that felt confining—it was the whole structure of family life. Her mother’s love was real, but it came with conditions. Every step toward independence seemed to trigger worry or disapproval. And even though her father wasn’t as involved in matters of faith, he still expected his daughter to protect the family’s reputation. The pressure to blend in, to follow the rules, was relentless. And the price of rebellion? It felt steep.
At school, these conflicts played out in new ways. Teachers rewarded obedience and punished anyone who dared to challenge the rules. The lessons were clear: respect authority, embrace tradition, do your duty. But the girl couldn’t ignore the contradictions she saw every day. Why were some voices encouraged and others silenced? Why were girls expected to be quiet and selfless, while boys were pushed to be bold and outspoken?
Questioning all of this wasn’t easy—it was painful. There were lonely moments, when it felt simpler just to give in and follow the rules. But there were also flashes of anger, when the unfairness of it all was just too much to ignore. She was stuck between wanting to fit in and needing to be true to herself.
In the middle of all this, conversations with friends became a lifeline. Some of them shared her doubts; others held tightly to their own sense of faith and tradition. These talks—intense, passionate, and sometimes confusing—made it clear that searching for meaning wasn’t just her struggle. It was something a lot of people wrestled with, even if they didn’t talk about it out loud.
Her relationship with her mother grew even more complicated. The love was always there, but so was a widening gap—her mother just couldn’t understand her need for independence. The girl craved acceptance, but mostly found disappointment instead. That distance between them hurt, but it also gave her the drive to keep searching for her own answers.
Over time, the need to obey started to fade, replaced by a deeper desire for authenticity. She realized that real faith—if it was even possible—couldn’t be forced on her from the outside. It had to come from within, chosen freely or not at all. The same went for loyalty, for duty, for love.
So, questioning her family and her faith wasn’t about turning her back on them—it was about trying to understand herself.
The journey wasn’t over. The battle between loyalty and independence, between belief and doubt, would go on for years. But those first steps? They mattered. Because now, she was no longer willing to just accept the world as it was. She wanted to know why things were the way they were—and whether, just maybe, they could be different.
